phases.title: Outside-In View
phases.subtitle: Arrive already understanding the industry
phases.intro: Desk work built on public information. Starting from nothing but the company URL, we build our own picture of how the industry makes money, why the best performers win, and where this client is likely losing value. The output is a hypothesis-led diagnostic pack, so the first leadership conversation is a validation session rather than a discovery session.
phases.note: Nothing here depends on client data or client time. Scope of work and the client’s own use cases do not enter the sprint until Phase 2.
participants: Strategy head / CEO office, if available
inputs: Company website URL
Sector, business segments and geographies
Latest annual report or investor presentation, where available
Public filings and financial disclosures, where the company is listed
Any competitor names the client considers relevant
Sector reports, trade press or analyst notes covering the industry
Altrd industry value tree and benchmark database for the sector
steps: Engagement opens - company URL received, nothing else
Desk research: site, filings, investor material, trade press
Build industry economics, value tree and value chain
Select comparables and pull benchmark metrics
Classify activities: differentiating, table stakes, service candidate
Form the hypothesis register and priority ranking
Draft questionnaires, data request list and stakeholder map
Internal review pass before anything reaches the client
Diagnostic pack carries into the leadership session

docs.name: Company Overview
docs.desc: Who the company is, what it sells and how it performs today.
sections: Company Snapshot - name, sector, headquarters, ownership, founding, headcount
Business Segments and Products - segment breakdown, product lines, revenue mix, growth by segment
Customers and Markets - customer types, concentration, end markets, order book
Geographies and Facilities - locations, plants, capacity and utilisation, domestic vs export
Production or Delivery Model - how value is produced, suppliers, make vs buy, systems used
Revenue and Financial Snapshot - revenue trend, growth, margins, cost ratios, working capital, capex
Organisation and Leadership - leadership team, reporting structure, functional heads
Recent Strategic Moves - investments, partnerships, acquisitions, stated technology direction
Key Observations - strengths, constraints, and what must be validated with leadership

docs.name: Industry Economics, Value Tree and Value Chain
docs.desc: How the industry makes money and where value sits.
sections: Industry Overview - definition, market size, growth, structural characteristics, segments
Industry Economics - core economic logic, margin structure, capital intensity, pricing dynamics
Value Tree: Revenue Drivers - demand, order wins, pricing, mix, capacity, utilisation, throughput, delivery, services
Value Tree: Cost Drivers - materials, procurement, labour, engineering, productivity, rework, quality, energy, logistics, overhead
Value Tree: Capital Drivers - inventory, receivables, payables, WIP, cycle time, asset utilisation, forecast accuracy
Industry Value Chain - per stage: activities, decisions, roles, inputs, outputs, systems, data, KPIs, economic impact
Key Value Pools - where value is created or lost, and which stages carry the most leverage
Implications for the Client - how the client maps onto the chain, and open questions

docs.name: Competitive Landscape and Benchmarks
docs.desc: Comparables, benchmarks and the client’s relative position.
sections: Competitor Set - selection criteria, the chosen comparables, rationale for each
Competitor Profiles - per competitor: overview, positioning, financials, footprint, differentiators
Benchmark Metrics - margin, growth, working capital, productivity, utilisation, execution, best performer per metric
Operating Model and Technology Comparison - structure, technology maturity, automation differentiators
AI and Digital Initiatives - announced programs, partnerships, vendor relationships
Services, Partnerships and New Business Models - new revenue streams, alliances, model innovation
Client Positioning vs Benchmarks - where stronger, where weaker, and initial explanations
Key Takeaways - competitive summary, value pool implications, open questions

docs.name: Activity Classification
docs.desc: What differentiates, what is table stakes, what could become a service.
sections: Classification Framework - definitions and the criteria applied
Full Activity Inventory - every activity by value chain stage, with a one-line description and classification
Differentiating Activities - where superior performance creates advantage, and why
Table Stakes Activities - suitability for automation, agentification, standardisation or elimination
Value-Added Service Opportunities - extensions that create new revenue, margin or customer value
Treatment Shortlists - consolidated candidates for automate, agentify, standardise, eliminate
Summary Matrix - activity vs classification vs recommended treatment

docs.name: Initial Hypotheses
docs.desc: What we believe before entering, and how we will test it.
sections: Methodology - how the hypotheses were formed and how the bank is used
Hypothesis Register - per hypothesis: ID, statement, external signal, suspected cause, validation metric, owning function, supporting questions
Hypotheses by Theme - revenue, cost, capital, operational, technology and AI readiness
Priority Hypotheses - highest impact or highest confidence, with rationale
Open Questions for the Leadership Session - including sensitive areas needing careful framing

docs.name: Questionnaires, Data Requests and Stakeholder Map
docs.desc: What to ask, what to collect, whom to speak to.
sections: Part A - Leadership Questionnaire: ambition, true competitors, margin drivers, constraints, strategic programs, perceived leakage, prior technology attempts
Part B - Department Questionnaires: per function, covering scale, efficiency, quality, business impact, pain points, systems and dependencies
Part C - Data Request List: per item, what it should contain, owning function, expected format, priority and due date
Part D - Stakeholder Map: per person, function, role in the process, influence, stake and interview priority

phases.title: Leadership Alignment
phases.subtitle: Reconcile our view with management’s
phases.intro: Phase 1 puts the outside-in view in front of leadership and tests it. We validate what management is actually trying to achieve, confirm which value drivers matter, resolve every hypothesis into confirmed, rejected or still open, and decide which functions Phase 2 will go deep on. Interviewing everyone is explicitly avoided.
phases.note: The single most important output is focus. Leaving this phase without a short list of priority functions means Phase 2 will sprawl.
participants: Altrd senior strategy lead and engagement lead
inputs: The Phase 0 diagnostic pack
Fathom recording and transcript of the promoter or CEO session
Notes and follow-ups from the leadership session
Completed leadership questionnaire responses
Org chart and reporting structure
Board deck, strategic plan or budget, where shareable
Prior consultant or technology reports, and what became of them
List of ongoing or planned strategic programs
steps: Leadership session with promoter or CEO, recorded on Fathom
Extract ambition, priorities, disputes and sensitivities from transcript
Correct the value tree with management’s own metric definitions
Resolve every hypothesis: confirmed, rejected or open
Confirm value pools and competitive gaps with leadership
Select priority functions and name process and data owners
Checkpoint: priority function list and access signed off

docs.name: Leadership Session Pack
docs.desc: What is put in front of the promoter or CEO.
sections: Outside-in summary - industry economics and how value is created
Benchmark position - client vs comparables on the metrics that matter
Competitive gaps - where the client trails, with initial explanations
Hypotheses for validation - framed as questions, not accusations
Discussion agenda and timings

docs.name: Management Ambition and Strategic Priorities
docs.desc: What leadership is actually trying to achieve.
sections: Stated 3 to 5 year ambition - growth, margin, scale, market position
Growth priorities - segments, geographies, products, channels
True competitors - who leadership benchmarks against, and why it may differ from ours
Margin drivers and constraints as management sees them
Ongoing strategic programs and their owners
Known value leakage and problem areas volunteered by leadership
Prior technology initiatives - what was attempted, what happened, what it cost politically
Sensitive areas and how they should be handled

docs.name: Validated Client Value Tree
docs.desc: The value tree, corrected by management.
sections: Confirmed revenue, cost and capital drivers for this specific business
Drivers explicitly deprioritised, with the reason
Metric definitions agreed - how the client actually calculates each one
Economics unique to this business that the industry tree did not capture
Data gaps - drivers nobody currently measures
Benchmark gaps carried into Phase 2

docs.name: Confirmed Value Pools and Competitive Gaps
docs.desc: Where the money is, agreed with leadership.
sections: Value pools ranked by size, with the basis of the estimate
Competitive gaps confirmed as real by management
Gaps management disputes, and what evidence would settle it
Constraints that cap what can be captured - capital, capacity, contracts, people
Initial view on which pools are addressable within the transformation

docs.name: Hypothesis Disposition Log
docs.desc: Every hypothesis resolved or scheduled.
sections: Per hypothesis: ID, statement, disposition (confirmed / rejected / open)
Evidence given in the session supporting the disposition
For open items: what data or interview will settle it, and in which phase
New hypotheses raised by leadership during the session
Revised priority ranking after the session

docs.name: Functional Priority and Phase 2 Scope Note
docs.desc: Where we go deeper, and where we deliberately do not.
sections: Priority functions and processes selected, with the rationale for each
Functions explicitly out of scope for this sprint
Named process owners and data owners per priority function
Data and access required before Phase 2 can start
Interview schedule and sequencing
Agreed timeline and checkpoints

phases.title: Functional Value Diagnosis
phases.subtitle: Replace anecdote with numbers
phases.intro: Phase 2 quantifies the problem. Across the priority functions we collect real volumes, cycle times, headcount, exception rates and costs, then attach a value pool to every issue. The phase ends with a scored opportunity universe and a shortlist of three to five processes worth forensic analysis.
phases.note: The discipline here is numeric. A pain point without a number attached is not yet an opportunity.
participants: Selected managers or analysts who own relevant data
inputs: Validated value tree and functional priorities from Phase 1
Scope of work and the use cases the client wants addressed
Completed department questionnaires for each priority function
Transaction, project and document volumes
Cycle times, approval counts, delays, rework and exception rates
Inventory, receivables, payables and working capital detail
Capacity, utilisation, order book and schedule adherence data
ERP, CRM and MIS exports, plus KPI dashboards
Fathom recordings and transcripts of functional head interviews
Altrd benchmark database and opportunity scoring model
steps: Issue questionnaires and the data request to each function
Functional head interviews, recorded on Fathom
Track arrivals, flag quality, record substitutions and assumptions
Build functional economics: scale, efficiency, quality, business impact
Attach a value pool to every issue, with the calculation basis
Score opportunities: value, pain, AI fit, feasibility, change complexity
Checkpoint: forensic shortlist of three to five processes agreed
Shortlist and value pools carry into Phase 3

docs.name: Data Request Tracker
docs.desc: What was asked for, what arrived, what is still missing.
sections: Item, description and owning function
Requested date, received date and current status
Quality flag - usable, partial, unreliable or refused
Substitutions and assumptions used where data was unavailable
Outstanding items escalated to leadership

docs.name: Functional Economics Pack
docs.desc: The numbers behind each priority function.
sections: Scale - people, cost, transactions, projects, documents handled
Efficiency - cycle time, productivity, cost per transaction, utilisation
Quality - errors, rework, rejection, exceptions, complaints
Business Impact - revenue, margin, working capital, capacity, customer experience, risk
Benchmark comparison where a comparable figure exists
Data quality notes and assumptions per metric

docs.name: Enterprise Opportunity Map
docs.desc: Every issue, quantified and placed.
sections: Issue statement and the function that owns it
Evidence - the numbers that establish it
Value pool attached, with the calculation basis
Root cause hypothesis
Which value tree driver it affects
Dependencies on other functions or systems

docs.name: Opportunity Scoring Sheet
docs.desc: How opportunities were ranked.
sections: Scoring criteria and the scale used for each
Business value score and rationale
Process pain score and rationale
AI suitability score and rationale
Feasibility score - data, systems, integration readiness
Change complexity score - people, process, politics
Weighted total and resulting rank

docs.name: Enterprise Opportunity Heatmap
docs.desc: The one-page view leadership reacts to.
sections: Function by value pool grid, shaded by priority
Top opportunities called out with their value at stake
Quick wins separated from structural plays
Areas deliberately parked, with the reason
Total quantified opportunity across the enterprise

docs.name: Forensic Shortlist
docs.desc: The three to five processes going into Phase 3.
sections: Process name, owning function and scope boundaries
Why it was selected - value, pain, AI fit, feasibility
Value pool at stake
Named process owner, managers and actual executors
Observation access required and any constraints
Proposed observation schedule

phases.title: Process Intelligence
phases.subtitle: Understand the work as it is actually done
phases.intro: Phase 3 is forensic. We watch the shortlisted processes being performed, follow a single real transaction from trigger to completion, and quantify every step. The goal is the real workflow with its workarounds and waiting, not the documented SOP.
phases.note: Documented process and actual process are rarely the same thing. What people do when the system is slow is usually where the value is.
participants: Altrd FDE, consultant and solution architect
inputs: Forensic shortlist and attached value pools from Phase 2
Observation notes from watching the work being performed
Fathom recordings and transcripts of process walkthroughs
Screen recordings or screenshots of the systems in use
A traced unit of work, from trigger through to completion
Sample documents and artefacts - tenders, drawings, purchase orders, invoices
Step-level timings: active effort, waiting time and volumes
Rework and exception data for the specific process
System and data owner input on what each system actually holds
Altrd friction taxonomy and step quantification template
steps: Shortlist and value pools in hand
Observe the work being performed, on site where possible
Trace one live transaction from trigger to completion
Collect screens, documents and artefacts as evidence
Quantify each step: effort, waiting, volume, rework, cost
Build the current-state process twin with real timings
Classify friction and resolve to root cause
Checkpoint: process owner confirms the twin is accurate
Twins and friction logs carry into Phase 4

docs.name: Observation Log and Evidence Pack
docs.desc: What was seen, with the proof.
sections: Session log - date, process, people observed, duration
Screens and systems used at each point
Documents and artefacts collected, indexed
Workarounds and shadow processes observed
Direct quotes capturing how people describe the work
Anything that contradicts the documented SOP

docs.name: Unit-of-Work Trace
docs.desc: One real transaction, end to end.
sections: Trigger event and how the work enters the process
Sequence of activities in the order they actually occurred
People and roles touching the work at each step
Decisions made, and on what basis
Handoffs and the mechanism of each - email, system, verbal, physical
Data movement between systems, including manual re-entry
Approvals, wait states and their durations
Exceptions encountered and how they were resolved
Total elapsed time vs total active effort

docs.name: Step Quantification Table
docs.desc: Every step, measured.
sections: Step name and owning role
Volume per period
Active effort per instance
Waiting time per instance
Number of people involved
Systems and data touched
Rework rate and exception rate
Cost per instance and annualised cost
Economic consequence of failure or delay at this step

docs.name: Current-State Process Twin
docs.desc: The workflow as it actually runs.
sections: End-to-end process diagram with real timings attached
Effort and cost overlaid per step
Systems and data flows shown, including manual bridges
Decision points and approval gates
Exception paths and their frequency
Cumulative cycle time vs value-adding time
Business impact of the process as it stands

docs.name: Friction Classification and Root Cause Log
docs.desc: Where the work is lost, and why.
sections: Friction type per step, using the standard taxonomy
Severity and frequency of each friction point
Effort and cost attributable to each friction type
Root cause - system, data, policy, skill, structure or incentive
Which frictions are symptoms of the same underlying cause
Candidate interventions flagged for Phase 4

phases.title: AI-Native Redesign
phases.subtitle: Rebuild the process from first principles
phases.intro: Phase 4 redesigns each priority process assuming current AI capability, rather than adding AI to the existing workflow. Every activity is challenged, handoffs are stripped out, decision rights are redrawn, and the split between human and AI responsibility is made explicit.
phases.note: The test for every activity is not “can AI help here” but “does this activity need to exist at all”.
participants: Altrd strategy lead, FDE, AI engineer and solution architect
inputs: Current-state process twins and friction logs from Phase 3
Scope and use cases confirmed in Phase 2
System landscape, integration options and API availability
Data availability, quality and where each dataset actually lives
Existing licences, vendor relationships and platform commitments
Non-negotiables - what cannot change, and why
Notes from design sessions with the process owner and IT
Altrd AI pattern library, agent architectures and integration patterns
steps: Twins and friction logs in hand
Challenge every activity: does it need to exist at all
Design session with the process owner and IT
Set dispositions: eliminate, automate, agentify, augment, retain
Draw the human and AI responsibility matrix
Redraw decision rights, thresholds and escalation routes
Draft the future-state flow and integration requirements
Checkpoint: IT confirms feasibility and constraints

docs.name: Activity Disposition Register
docs.desc: Every activity, and what happens to it.
sections: Activity name, current owner and current effort
Disposition - eliminate, automate, agentify, augment or retain
Rationale for the disposition
What replaces it, if anything
Effort and cycle time released
Dependencies and prerequisites
Risk introduced and how it is mitigated

docs.name: Current vs Future State Comparison
docs.desc: The before and after, side by side.
sections: Activity count - current vs future
Handoff count - current vs future
Approval count - current vs future
Total effort per instance - current vs future
Cycle time - current vs future
Exception and rework rates - current vs future
Headcount effect and capacity released
Summary of what structurally changed and why

docs.name: Human and AI Responsibility Matrix
docs.desc: Who does what in the new process.
sections: What AI monitors and detects
What AI retrieves and assembles
What AI reasons about and recommends
What AI generates - documents, drafts, plans, responses
What AI executes autonomously
What AI coordinates across systems and people
What AI escalates, and on what trigger
What humans decide, approve, negotiate, review and own as exceptions
Accountability - who remains responsible for the outcome

docs.name: Decision Rights and Escalation Model
docs.desc: Where authority sits in the redesigned process.
sections: Decision inventory - every decision in the process
Decision owner in the future state - AI, human or joint
Thresholds and limits on autonomous action
Escalation triggers and routes
Audit and traceability requirements per decision
Override and reversal mechanisms
Governance review cadence

docs.name: Future-State Process Design
docs.desc: The redesigned process itself.
sections: End-to-end future-state process flow
Activities retained, augmented, agentified and automated, marked on the flow
New KPIs and how they are measured
Data and integration requirements per step
Failure modes and fallback paths
Transition considerations from current to future state
Expected economic impact of the redesign

docs.name: Solution and Integration Requirements
docs.desc: What has to be built for this to work.
sections: Systems to be integrated and the direction of each flow
Data required, its source, quality and any gaps
Interfaces and user touchpoints
AI capability requirements per step
Evaluation and quality assurance approach
Governance, access control and audit requirements
Assumptions and open technical risks

phases.title: Business Case & Portfolio
phases.subtitle: Turn design into an investment decision
phases.intro: Phase 5 converts the redesign into money and sequence. Each initiative gets a business case with investment, return and payback. The portfolio is sorted into now, next, later and do not build, then sequenced by dependency so the client does not end up with disconnected AI projects.
phases.note: A ranked portfolio with dependencies is the deliverable. A list of good ideas without a sequence is not implementable.
participants: Altrd engagement, strategy, solution and commercial leads
inputs: Future-state designs and requirements from Phase 4
Existing licence, infrastructure and vendor costs
Finance assumptions - hurdle rate, payback expectation, capitalisation policy
Budget envelope and approval thresholds
IT roadmap and initiatives already committed
Change management capacity and training constraints
Altrd ROI benchmarks, implementation effort library and rate card
steps: Cost each initiative: build, integration, licences, change, run
Quantify benefit, payback and total value at stake
Sort the portfolio: NOW, NEXT, LATER, DO NOT BUILD
Sequence by dependency and mark the critical path
Specify implementation scope for the NOW initiatives
CFO review of assumptions, rates and sensitivities
Checkpoint: portfolio approved as an investment decision
Altrd AI Transformation Blueprint assembled and handed over

docs.name: Business Case per Initiative
docs.desc: The money case for each intervention.
sections: Current state cost - effort, delay, rework, errors, leakage, working capital, capacity constraint
Future state benefit - effort reduction, cycle time, productivity, capacity, revenue, margin, working capital
Investment - build, integration, infrastructure, licences, change management, ongoing run cost
Return - annual benefit, payback period, ROI, total value at stake
Assumptions and their sensitivity
Risks and what would invalidate the case
Confidence rating on the estimate

docs.name: KPI Framework
docs.desc: How success will be measured after go-live.
sections: KPI name and precise definition
Current baseline and how it was established
Target and the date by which it should be met
Measurement source and frequency
Owner accountable for the metric
Link back to the value tree driver it moves
Leading indicators that will show progress early

docs.name: Transformation Portfolio
docs.desc: Everything sorted into now, next, later or never.
sections: NOW - high value, feasible and ready, with the reason each qualifies
NEXT - high potential but dependent on something landing first
LATER - useful but not currently important enough
DO NOT BUILD - low ROI, poor data, mismatch or unnecessary complexity, with the reason stated
Portfolio-level investment and return summary
Total value at stake across the program

docs.name: Transformation Sequence and Dependency Map
docs.desc: The order things must happen in.
sections: Initiative sequence across the program timeline
Dependencies between initiatives, technical and organisational
Foundational enablers that must land first - data, integration, platform
Critical path and the consequence of slipping it
Resourcing and capability required per stage
Decision points and stage gates
Quick wins positioned to build credibility early

docs.name: Implementation Scope for NOW Initiatives
docs.desc: What gets built first, specified.
sections: Business objective and the outcome being bought
Users, roles and the workflow being changed
Functional requirements
AI requirements and capability needed
Data, integrations and interfaces
Governance, security and audit requirements
KPIs and acceptance criteria
Timeline, milestones and team composition
Indicative commercial requirement
